explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves DONE_IN_PROC row-count messages enabled for every statement in usp_TestProcedure, adding network chatter and breaking some client result-set handling.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF while the procedure uses explicit transactions (lines 181, 238) allows run-time errors to leave a partially applied, open transaction.
SELECT * FROM Sales.Orders returns all 17 columns including three nvarchar(MAX) fields, coupling callers to schema changes and wasting I/O.
SELECT TOP (10) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so the 10 rows returned are arbitrary and can change between executions.
DISTINCT on o.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders; it forces a needless aggregate/sort.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders permits dirty reads, missing rows and duplicated rows during page splits.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2016 wraps the date column in a function, preventing a range seek; use OrderDate >= '20160101' AND OrderDate < '20170101'.
o.CustomerID (int) is compared to @CustomerIdText (nvarchar(20)), forcing an implicit conversion driven by data-type precedence and risking conversion failures.
@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID produces a catch-all plan that scans Sales.Orders instead of seeking on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
LIKE N'%urgent%' on o.Comments (nvarchar(MAX)) cannot seek any index and scans the whole Orders table.
NOT IN against SELECT i.CustomerID FROM Sales.Invoices is NULL-sensitive: any NULL introduced by the subquery (e.g. after an outer join or schema change) makes the whole predicate return no rows.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps the indexed CustomerID column, blocking an index seek; CustomerID is NOT NULL so the wrapper is also pointless.
o.OrderID + 0 = @OrderID performs arithmetic on the primary key column, preventing a clustered index seek.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is an inequality that matches nearly every row and forces a broad scan of Sales.Orders.
CROSS JOIN of Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate, producing a row count equal to Orders x Customers before TOP (1) is applied.
Comma-separated FROM Sales.Orders AS o, Sales.OrderLines AS ol with the join condition in WHERE uses deprecated join syntax and hides the join predicate.
The correlated COUNT(*) over Sales.OrderLines is evaluated once per Orders row; a single GROUP BY join or OUTER APPLY would compute all counts in one pass.
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID AND ol.Quantity > 1) is a per-row correlated probe that can be written as a set-based semi-join/derived aggregate.
The CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END expression is duplicated in the select list and ORDER BY, so it is maintained twice and may be computed twice.
ORDER BY 2 depends on the position of o.OrderDate in the select list and silently sorts a different column if the list is edited.
OFFSET/FETCH ordered only by o.OrderDate, which is not unique in Sales.Orders, so page boundaries are unstable; add OrderID as a tie-breaker.
The two branches filter OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 on the same key, so they are disjoint; UNION adds a needless distinct sort.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts every matching line instead of stopping at the first row as EXISTS would.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders assigns from an unordered multi-row set, silently keeping an arbitrary last value and leaving @OrderID unchanged when no rows exist.
@OrderIds table variable has no column statistics and gets a 1-row (or fixed) estimate, producing poor plans if it is loaded with many OrderIDs.
INSERT ... SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so which five OrderIDs land in @OrderIds is arbitrary.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp table implicitly, taking schema locks in tempdb and hiding the column definitions.
TOP (5) without ORDER BY makes the contents of #ImplicitOrders nondeterministic.
order_cursor iterates Sales.Orders one OrderID at a time (OPEN/FETCH at lines 97-98) for work expressible as a single set-based statement.
The WHILE @Counter <= 1 loop performs iterative counter work in T-SQL instead of a set-based operation.
@Sql is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @CustomerID) into the command text, preventing plan reuse and embedding values in SQL.
EXEC (@Sql) executes a concatenated string with no parameter binding, so each distinct CustomerID compiles a separate plan.
@Sql is again assembled by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @OrderID) into the statement text rather than using a parameter placeholder.
sys.sp_executesql is called with only @Sql and no parameter definition list, so the embedded OrderID value is not bound and plans are not reused.
#Scratch is created but never dropped, keeping tempdb objects alive until the procedure scope ends.
The CATCH block only SELECTs ERROR_MESSAGE() as IgnoredError; the failure (e.g. the divide-by-zero path at line 121) is hidden from the caller and no THROW or failure status is returned.
RAISERROR (N'Negative order ID', 16, 1) uses legacy error syntax; THROW preserves the original error and honours XACT_ABORT/TRY-CATCH semantics.
PRINT N'Monster procedure diagnostic' is buffered output that mixes with result sets and cannot be consumed as structured diagnostics.
o.CustomerID = 1 embeds a specific business identifier instead of using the @CustomerID parameter already declared.
o.OrderDate >= '20160101' hard-codes an unlabelled date boundary in query logic rather than a named parameter or documented constant.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') has no style argument, so the value depends on the session DATEFORMAT/language and can mean Jan 2 or Feb 1 (or fail).
COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) = COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) wraps both join keys, blocking index seeks on the CustomerID indexes and matching all NULL customers to each other.
Sales.Orders is joined to itself on OrderID = OrderID only to return o.OrderID, which is already available from the single row; the join adds a redundant seek.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts an nvarchar(MAX) LOB column across all orders, causing large memory grants and likely tempdb spills.
SUM(ol.Quantity) scans the entire fact-like Sales.OrderLines table with no WHERE restriction to produce one scalar.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 filters a grouping key at row level; it belongs in WHERE so rows are eliminated before the aggregate.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns exactly one row, so ORDER BY OrderCount adds nothing.
MERGE into Sales.Orders has documented concurrency/upsert race and key-change issues; separate UPDATE and IF NOT EXISTS INSERT is safer.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments writes the current value back, incurring locking, logging and versioning for no data change.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 removes rows by a non-key business value, potentially deleting an unbounded number of order lines.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks the worker thread and holds the session (and any locks) instead of using asynchronous scheduling.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is issued outside any TRY/CATCH, so an error between BEGIN and ROLLBACK can leave an open transaction holding locks.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON changes session-scoped state and couples the procedure to manual identity management on a shared table.
EXEC sp_who is not schema-qualified (and uses the sp_ prefix), causing extra resolution overhead and possible name collisions.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is never reset to 0, so every subsequent statement in the session (including the later INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) is silently limited to one row.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (99, @NewCategory) omits the column list, so the insert breaks or misaligns if the temp table definition changes.
CategoryID 99 is a magic business identifier embedded in the VALUES clause instead of being passed in or looked up.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' starts with a wildcard, so UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName cannot be seeked and Sales.Customers is scanned.
@CustomerName (caller-supplied nvarchar) is concatenated straight into the dynamic LIKE string, allowing quote-breaking SQL injection when executed at line 220.
EXEC sp_executesql is called without the sys schema qualifier, relying on name resolution for a system routine.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 has no WHERE clause and overwrites the category for every loaded customer row.
CustomerCategoryID = 1 is a hard-coded business identifier rather than a parameter or lookup value.
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' filters the LEFT JOINed Sales.Orders side, discarding NULL-extended rows and effectively turning the outer join into an inner join.
'2016-01-01' is an unlabelled date constant embedded in the filter instead of a named date parameter.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL never evaluates to true under ANSI nulls, so the query always returns zero rows; use IS NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the select list is a scalar UDF evaluated per customer row and blocks parallelism unless the function is inlined.
The CATCH for the transaction opened at line 238 never rolls back, leaving an open or doomed transaction that holds locks after the procedure returns.
The CATCH block only SELECTs ERROR_MESSAGE(); it neither rethrows with THROW nor returns a failure status, so the DELETE failure is invisible to the caller.
WITH (INDEX = 1) pins Sales.Customers to a specific index id, which is fragile across index rebuilds/reordering and prevents the optimizer from choosing a better plan.
Three levels of nested derived tables (t1/t2/t3) wrap the same simple CustomerID projection, obscuring the query; refactor to a CTE or a single query.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' in the innermost derived table forces a full scan of Sales.Customers.
SELECT * FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) exposes every function output column and breaks callers if the function's table schema changes.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement TVF: it is optimized with a fixed row estimate and its body is executed separately, unlike an inline TVF that is folded into the outer query.
